title: A secure base
hookLine: Bowlby and Ainsworth found children thrive with a secure base to explore from

cards: A park bench, and on it a parent with a coffee. Out in front, a small child heads off toward the sandbox, stops, looks back. Still there.
Goes a little farther, to the slide. Looks back again. Still there.

Then off to the far swings, completely absorbed. Anyone who has watched a small child play may know this little loop: go, check, go farther. Two researchers studied it closely, and one of them is today's word.

teach.b: The psychiatrist John Bowlby argued that a child's tie to a caregiver isn't just about food. It's a bond of its own, built to keep the child close to safety. He called it attachment.
The psychologist Mary Ainsworth watched how young children behaved when their caregiver was in the room, left the room, and came back.

Children with a secure attachment used the caregiver as a base: they explored freely, came back for comfort when upset, then went out exploring again. Bowlby later titled a book after the idea: A Secure Base.
And the securely attached children weren't the clingy ones. Feeling safe is what made them brave enough to wander. Love, in this picture, isn't a fence.

An old picture of it sits in Psalm 131, in the Bible: "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child." Not a baby crying to be fed.
A child near its mother, and calm.
Bowlby held that people of every age need a secure base. Adults need someone to come back to, too.

how: Attachment research, from John Bowlby and Mary Ainsworth onward, describes how children explore from a trusted caregiver and return for comfort; parents, teachers and therapists use the idea of a secure base to support children and adults.

practice: Think of someone who has been a secure base for you, a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend, anyone whose steadiness made it easier to try things, and let yourself remember their face.
Then turn it around: think of one person who might use you that way, a child, a friend in a hard stretch, a new colleague, and ask what it would take to be the bench they can look back to.
